summary: Overall the course is accurate and well structured. I recomputed every numeric key (feasibility, inclusion-exclusion, RR/NNT, sample-size, design-effect, retention months, word budgets, percentages, medians) and all agree with the keys and tolerances; MCQ keys each have a single correct option, and I found no list items that are empty or a literal [object Object]. The two substantive problems are both in lesson worked examples: an arithmetic error in the triglyceride mean, and a risk/odds mix-up in the relative-risk interpretation. The remaining issues are minor consistency and clarity points. This is an AI review only: the course still needs a subject-matter expert (research methods and biostatistics) before reliance, and the statistical p-values and CIs in the worked examples were checked only by approximate recalculation.

issues.problem: Worked example on triglycerides: "Add the values to get a total of 14.1 mmol/L ... mean = 14.1/9 = 1.57". The nine values (1.0, 1.1, 1.2, 1.2, 1.3, 1.4, 1.5, 1.6, 4.8) sum to 15.1, so the mean is 1.68, not 1.57. The final answer repeats "Mean = 1.57 mmol/L". The median (1.3) is correct.
issues.suggestedFix: Change the total to 15.1 mmol/L and the mean to 15.1/9 = 1.68 mmol/L in the step and in the answer (or change a data value so the stated total holds). The conclusion that the median is preferable is unaffected.

issues.problem: Worked example on relative risk: "the app group had 75% higher odds of passing in relative terms". The statistic computed (21/70 divided by 12/70 = 1.75) is a relative risk, not an odds ratio; the odds ratio here would be about 2.1. Conflating risk and odds teaches a misconception.
issues.suggestedFix: Say "75% higher risk (probability) of passing in relative terms" or "a relative risk of 1.75".

issues.problem: Scenario has 8 tutorial groups of about 10 students (about 80 students), yet the adjusted sample to plan is 407. The arithmetic (DE = 1.27, 320 x 1.27 = 406.4 to 407) is correct, but the stem implies a pool that cannot supply 407 participants.
issues.suggestedFix: Change the stem to something like "tutorial groups of about 10 students, with enough groups available" or increase the number of groups (about 41 clusters) so the scenario is coherent.

issues.problem: Worked example on rewriting an abstract: the model Background says "Sleep or teaching interventions may affect short-term performance", although the study is about hand-hygiene teaching and quiz scores (sleep is irrelevant). The Results line also puts a limitation ("although the sample was small") in Results, and the original text gives no results numbers.
issues.suggestedFix: Rewrite Background as e.g. "Short teaching sessions may improve hand-hygiene knowledge in medical students"; move "small sample" to the Conclusion/limitations.

issues.problem: Table lists CONSORT for "Randomised controlled trials and other intervention trials". CONSORT is for randomised trials; non-randomised intervention studies are reported with TREND. The unit objective (select the correct guideline) is also covered only for CONSORT versus STROBE, although distractors such as PRISMA, SPIRIT, CARE, ARRIVE appear in questions without being introduced.
issues.suggestedFix: Restrict the CONSORT row to randomised trials (note TREND for non-randomised designs). Add one line mentioning PRISMA (systematic reviews), SPIRIT (protocols), CARE (case reports), ARRIVE (animal studies) or avoid them as distractors.

issues.problem: The Boolean set-operations formula ends with "\setminus C" but C is never defined and NOT is only discussed elsewhere as something to avoid. Also worked example 1 says the outcome block is kept "only if important for precision", yet the string includes delirium.
issues.suggestedFix: Define C as the excluded set (the NOT block) or remove it from the formula; reword the worked example step to say why the delirium block is included or optional.

issues.problem: Option c) is "PubMed" while the stem asks for a source "in addition to PubMed", so that option is not a plausible distractor; Google Scholar and CINAHL are also not well-argued wrong options.
issues.suggestedFix: Replace option c with a different plausible source (for example Embase alone as an alternative) or reword the stem.

issues.problem: Questions q001 and q006 offer "Measurement gap" as a distractor, but the lesson table names the fourth gap type "Methodological gap".
issues.suggestedFix: Use "Methodological gap" in the options so terminology matches the lesson.

issues.problem: The worked example prompt asks for "two specific objectives" but the steps list three numbered objectives, and the final answer gives only two (with measure-baseline and compare merged).
issues.suggestedFix: Make the steps and the answer both show two objectives (or ask for three).

issues.problem: The stem treats a ten-minute slot as 8 minutes of speaking plus 2 minutes of questions, whereas the lesson, objective and q002/q006 treat the ten-minute talk as 10 minutes of speaking (1200 words at 120 wpm).
issues.suggestedFix: Align the time structure across the unit, e.g. state that the talk is 10 minutes plus separate question time, or adapt the lesson word budget.

issues.problem: Categorical worked example answer says "Most students preferred morning study time", but morning is 14 of 36 (38.9%), a plurality rather than a majority.
issues.suggestedFix: Say "The largest group (38.9%) preferred morning study time" or "More students preferred morning than any other time".

issues.problem: Key and explanation describe d = 0.70 as a "moderate effect"; by Cohen's conventions 0.5 is medium and 0.8 large, so 0.7 is medium-to-large. The stem also omits a p-value though option c refers to "the p-value alone".
issues.suggestedFix: Say "a medium-to-large point estimate" and keep the emphasis on the CI width; optionally remove the p-value reference in option c.
